title: Looking back: the streams
hookLine: many streams and places, one Guru

lines: OR THE GURDWARA DOWN THE ROAD.
cards: If you could stand in one Sikh place for a single hour, which would it be? Nankana Sahib, where tradition places Guru Nanak's birth. Kartarpur, where tradition says he farmed in his last years.
Anandpur, where the Khalsa began. Hemkunt, up among snow and a cold lake. Or somewhere much closer: the gurdwara a short drive away, folding tables stacked against the wall for langar.
This year walked through those places, and the many streams of Sikh life that gather in them. Today, a look back at both, and at what runs through all of them.

teach.b: First, the streams differ, and that's real. The Udasis kept a life of renunciation. The Nirmalas gave themselves to learning.
The Nihangs keep their blue and their old ways of speech. The Namdharis wear white.
There are Sindhi devotees of Nanak, Sikh families in Assam, communities shaped by craft and trade, and Sikhs in the West who came to the path as adults.
Different dress, tunes and emphases, and nobody had to pretend those differences away.

Second, places hold memory. A gurdwara often stands where something happened: a birth, a field worked, a stand taken, a death. Sikhs travel to them to remember, and to sit where the Gurus' story touched the ground.
Third, the thread. Walk into one of those halls at dawn.

teach.h: THE SAME GRANTH OPENED AT DAWN.
teach.b: Someone lifts the cloths from the Guru Granth Sahib, and the day begins with its word, in the same Gurmukhi letters. The snow differs, the language of the street differs, the food in the langar differs.
The book at the center is the one this path has read all year. Fourth, the Granth gives a line for walking between streams.
Guru Arjan writes, in paraphrase: no one is my enemy, and no one is a stranger; I have come to get along with everyone.
That's a fair way to visit another sangat: not to rank it or correct it, but to sit down, cover your head, and listen.
Many streams, many places. And in the gurdwaras this path visited this year, one Guru open at the center.

how: Sikhs from many streams travel to historic gurdwaras to remember the Gurus' lives, and in gurdwaras near and far the day begins with the Guru Granth Sahib opened and read.

o: a year-end look at Sikh streams and places, one Granth
a pilgrimage to every gurdwara the Gurus founded
a call for every Sikh group to dress the same way

games.q: streams and places from the year: tap the pairs.

s: to honor the streams, you have to pretend they're all the same
the streams really differ in dress, tunes and emphasis; nobody had to pretend that away.
Guru Arjan writes that no one is his enemy and no one a stranger
he has come, he says, to get along with everyone.
the day in a gurdwara begins with the Guru Granth Sahib opened
someone lifts the cloths, and the day begins with its word.

games.q: you're visiting a sangat from a stream you don't know. their dress and tunes are new to you. what do you do?
o: point out what they're doing differently.
sit down, cover your head, and listen.
leave and find a gurdwara like yours.
games.why: Guru Arjan's line fits: no one is my enemy, no one a stranger. the Granth at the center is the same one.

practice: Bring one place from this year to mind, or a gurdwara near you: the door, shoes off, head covered, hands washed, the Granth under its canopy.
Ask what you'd do first, sit for kirtan, bow, or wash plates in the langar, and stay there a while, doing that one thing. If you pray, carry a prayer in with you.

wordCard.voice: Looking back. Today, at the streams and the places: real differences, real memories, and the same Granth opened at the center. Today's word.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: sangat, the gathering that sits together before the Guru's word, wherever it meets.

carryVoice: Your line: many streams. Real differences, one Granth at the center, and no one a stranger. Until tomorrow.
